items.title: Node.js Queue Design for Webhook Follow-Up Tasks One Hour Later
items.summary: Short answer: for a webhook follow-up that is due one hour later, record a durable obligation keyed by the source event, let workers claim due work, and reserve cron for recurring reconciliation rather than creating a cron entry for each event. The decision is less about a Node.js library than about what remains true after the request handler has exited, a process has been redeployed, and the upstream sender has retried the same webhook. A delayed message, a database-backed queue, and a scheduled scan can all initiate work; none removes the need to identify the logical action once, preserve its history, and verify its outcome. For payment- or ledger-adjacent systems, that distinction is consequential: a timer is not evidence that an obligation was accepted. One durable record changes the question from "did a timer fire?" to "which accepted event still lacks an explained terminal state?" That is a question an operator can query, audit, and reconcile. Treat the incoming webhook as an input to a transaction, not as permission to start a process-local clock. items.title: Rounding clock times to the nearest 15 minutes: what the law allows and what I coded
items.summary: Most people who clock in at 8:58 do not expect to be paid from 9:00. And most people who clock in at 9:07 do not expect to be paid from 9:00 either, though that is exactly what happens on a lot of time cards. Rounding is one of those small payroll features that looks trivial until you write it, because the rule is not "round everything" — it is round fairly, and prove it. Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, an employer may round clock times to the nearest 5 minutes, the nearest tenth of an hour, or the nearest quarter of an hour, as long as the rounding does not, over time, favour the employer. That is the whole test. The regulation — 29 CFR 785.48(b) — does not say "always round down" or "always round to the nearest". It says the practice must average out, so it cannot systematically shave minutes off every shift. The classic example is the 15-minute rule. A clock-in at 8:53 rounds to 8:45. A clock-in at 8:54 rounds to 9:00. The cut-off sits at 7 minutes and 30 seconds past the quarter, which in practice means 7 minutes either way. If your system rounds 8:53 to 8:45 but also rounds 9:07 to 9:00, the worker gains on one side and loses on the other, and over a month it balances.

items.title: Do not pretty-print, lint-fix, or re-minify MeowShield output
items.summary: A MeowShield-protected file is not a normal source artifact. It is the output of a transform you chose, with a shape that later tools may not understand. The instinct to "clean it up" is strong: run Prettier so the diff looks tidy, run ESLint with --fix, send it through Terser "one more time" to recover a few bytes, or paste it into an editor that helpfully rewrites quotes and line breaks. Those tools were built for human-written JavaScript. They can change, or simply break, the file you just protected. I help promote MeowShield. The rule I would put in the repo is: once MeowShield has produced a file, that file is frozen. You may upload it, hash it, and serve it. You may not format it, lint-fix it, or pack it again. The output can look noisy. Identifiers are renamed, constants may be split, control flow may be less linear, and a stronger level can look unlike the module you reviewed in the pull request. A well-meaning reviewer asks for "just a format pass." A size-conscious release job already minifies everything in dist/, and the protected file sits in that folder. items.title: Your Workspace Package's `.npmrc` Does Nothing. The Root File Decides Everything
items.summary: Four installs. Four hooks ran. The warning showed up twice, and both times in the one place where it could do nothing at all. cryptostrapon asked this one in the comments on my last npm piece, and it is the sharpest edge in the whole series so far. He runs a workspaces monorepo where three files disagree. The root file says hooks may run. The package's own file, inside packages/a, says they may not. His user file says they may not too. From a root install, npm printed that it was ignoring the workspace config at packages/a/.npmrc, and the package's install hook ran anyway. His point was not that the root wins. We already knew the root wins. His point was that a check inside the package reads green and tells you nothing, because the root file plus env and flags are what decide, and the package file is not even part of the conversation. I rebuilt his shape and ran it on npm 10.9.4 with Node v24.22.1. The monorepo is one root package.json with a packages/* workspace, one package called pkg-a, and three config files that disagree about one setting: the user file and the package file switch install hooks off, the root file switches them on. user file (~/.npmrc): ignore-scripts=true root

items.title: Triage flow for Xcode 16 and Swift 6 concurrency errors without leaving the IDE
items.summary: Swift 6 concurrency errors are the most expensive English text a macOS developer reads. A single MainActor isolation mistake can produce a wall of text spanning twenty lines, each a separate diagnostic with its own file and line reference. You copy it, lose a few lines to the wrapping, and now your clipboard holds an error message instead of the fragment you were about to paste. This is a triage flow for Xcode 16 / Swift 6 diagnostics that keeps you inside the IDE: read the root diagnostic first, work out which concurrency shape it is, then fix code. Isolation violation — mutation of captured var 'x' in concurrently-executing code. A captured value is mutated across actor boundaries; the note underneath names the isolation the closure requires. Sendable conformance — type 'Foo' does not conform to the 'Sendable' protocol. Something crosses an isolation domain while holding non-Sendable state. Global actor mismatch — main actor-isolated property 'y' can not be referenced from a nonisolated context. Typically a @MainActor type touched from a background task. items.title: The Impact of WebFormsJS on Web Pages
items.summary: What is WebFormsJS WebFormsJS is a lightweight JavaScript library developed by Elanat that extends the capabilities of standard HTML pages by providing client-side features such as AJAX navigation, SPA behavior, automatic form submission, page state management, and communication handling, without requiring a specific server-side framework. It is also the client-side execution engine of WebForms Core (WFC), a server-driven UI manipulation technology designed to coordinate interactions between the server and the browser. WebForms Core follows a stateless architecture in which the server does not render dynamic HTML or maintain a server-side DOM tree. Instead, it generates commands that WebFormsJS interprets and executes directly against the browser's DOM. Together, these technologies provide an approach to web development in which the server orchestrates UI operations while the client handles their execution. Note: WebFormsJS is present in the core CodeBehind framework. However, you can use it in other backend frameworks. Installation via Package JavaScript in npm (https://www.npmjs.com/package/webformsjs) CLI npm install webformsjs Download from the Elanat website https://elanat.net

items.title: Switching classes on button press is just state
items.summary: The first dark mode toggle I built in React, I built the way I had built them in plain JavaScript for years. I grabbed the document body and called classList.toggle('dark') on it, and it worked. Click, dark. Click again, light. It shipped, and then a user reported the toggle losing its setting. They would switch to dark, click anything that re-rendered the page, and the page snapped back to light while the button still said dark. The class and the state had disagreed, and the class lost, because React re-renders from state, not from anything painted onto the DOM by hand. The rule: in React, a class is not something you apply, it is something state decides. The button does not change its own class, it changes a value, and the render picks the class that matches. Treat className as a function of state, and every toggle, tab bar, and theme picker gets simpler, because there is only ever one thing to update. The simplest case is one button with two looks, and a boolean in useState is all the state it needs. The className reads the boolean with a ternary, and the label reads the same boolean, so the look and the words can never disagree. ThemeToggle.tsx import { useState } from 'react';

items.title: State lives in the parent, the child just asks
items.summary: The SeatFinder check-in button lives in the guest row. It is a small thing, one button per guest, and the checked-in state looks like it belongs right there next to it, inside the row component. Put it there and the button works, it flips to Checked in on tap, while the header count says 0 of 80 where it should say 3 of 80. The row knew. The parent had no idea. (The row knew, the parent had no idea, and that gap was the bug.) The tempting next move is worse: change the prop directly from the child, as if the row could reach up and rewrite what the parent passed down. React ignores it. Props are read-only by design, and a child that mutates them is writing on a copy that nobody re-reads. One-way data flow is not a diagram in the docs, it is the rule that decides where state is allowed to live. The fix has a name in the React docs, lifting state up, and it is simpler than it sounds. The state moves into the closest parent that needs to see it, and the parent passes a callback down to the child. The child calls the callback when something happens, the parent updates the state, and the new value flows back down as a prop. Props go down, callbacks go up, and the circle is complete. Here

items.title: Earth has a New Moon
items.summary: "Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN: Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. items.summary: Working with PDFs in .NET used to mean juggling a few different libraries. One to create files. One to read text. Another to turn pages into images. Each had its own style and its own quirks. I got tired of that. So I built NetPdfKit. It puts all of that behind one simple, fluent API. NetPdfKit is a .NET library for creating, reading, and managing PDF files. Under the hood, it uses well-known open-source libraries: PDFsharp, PdfPig, PDFtoImage, ZXing.Net, and Svg.Skia. You don't need to learn each one. You learn one API, and it does the rest. Works on Windows, macOS, and Linux Supports .NET 8, 9, 10, and 11 MIT licensed There are three packages. items.title: Reading unselectable Xcode/Unity errors: rectangle OCR with Apple Vision on macOS
items.summary: Xcode and Unity errors are often visible on screen but impossible to select. Runtime crash dialogs, plugin warnings rendered by native UI, Electron renderer panes — ⌘C returns nothing because these surfaces are not text views. If your translation workflow depends on the clipboard, it silently dies there. This is an implementation note on reading those errors with Apple Vision (VNRecognizeTextRequest) from a screen rectangle: how to capture, how to convert coordinates, how to reduce misreads, and where the approach honestly stops. CGWindowListCreateImage lets you grab a single window, which is less noisy than the full desktop. It is deprecated from macOS 14 onward, so treat it as a fallback. SCScreenshotManager / SCStream is the current path, available per-window and per-display. It is async, which makes cancellation easier when the user re-triggers the shortcut. Both require Screen Recording permission, and both fail silently without it: the call succeeds and returns an image of the wallpaper. items.summary: A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports: A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins. items.title: Win + click to convert any file: building a WinUI 3 app that lives in Explorer
items.summary: I build Morphalo, a Windows 11 utility with one idea: you shouldn't have to open a converter. Hold the Windows key, click a file in File Explorer, and a ring of actions (the Halo) opens around it with every conversion and tool that fits that file. Pick one. The original stays untouched; the new file waits beside it. This post is about the parts that were interesting to build: catching a modifier-click globally without breaking the shell, an Explorer context-menu entry that can't crash Explorer, and keeping heavy native libraries out of the UI process. The gesture needs a global hook: WH_KEYBOARD_LL to track the modifier chord and WH_MOUSE_LL to see the click. Both run on a dedicated thread with its own message loop, because low-level hooks are called on the installing thread and Windows silently removes a hook that is slow to return. The rule I ended up enforcing in code review: hook callbacks do no allocations, no COM and no logging. They update a tiny chord state machine, and if the chord matches, they post a message to a separate probe thread and return immediately. items.title: 3 App Review rejections in one week, and the exact fix for each (ATT, China, privacy manifest)
items.summary: I'm a solo developer and I submitted three iOS apps to App Review in the same week: a prayer-times app (Flutter), a PDF password remover and an expense tracker (both SwiftUI). Between them I collected three rejections and one launch crash on TestFlight. None of them were exotic, and each one cost me a 24–48 hour review cycle, so here is what happened and what fixed it. What I did wrong. My apps show a few native ads, so I declared tracking in App Privacy. But I only called requestTrackingAuthorization right before the first ad load. And to give the reviewer a calm first impression, I had set a Remote Config flag that disabled ads for the first 24 hours. So the reviewer opened the app, saw no ad, never saw the ATT prompt, and rejected the build under 2.1: App Privacy said the app tracks, but the reviewer could not find the permission request. Fix. Ask ATT shortly after onboarding finishes, independent of whether an ad will load. Order: UMP consent form (if required in the region) → ATT → only then start the ads SDK. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. items.title: FCC Backs AT&T's Plan To Remove Copper Landlines In California
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. In May, the company urged the commission to declare that federal laws preempted California's regulations, thus clearing the way for AT&T to discontinue the service as it prioritizes high-speed fiber and expanded 5G cellular coverage. Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. The figure surpasses the lifetime global box-office earnings of Avengers: Endgame ($2.9 billion) and comes after more than a decade of development at a reported cost of $1.5 billion. The game developer declined to disclose the number of 'GTA 6' copies sold. "It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of 'Grand Theft Auto VI,'" Rockstar Games president and founder Sam Houser said. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn't be more excited to share this moment with you." We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “no way”. Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger. Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: OpenAI's ‘shepherds' affirm blockbuster physics result (3 minute read)
items.summary: Experts appointed by OpenAI have verified OpenAI's proof of the existence of the quantum Yang-Mills theory, a vital foundation for the Standard Model of particle physics. OpenAI created a committee to supervise the proof's release after backlash it received when it released a flood of more than 700 AI-generated proofs on a single day in October. This shepherding approach has riled some mathematicians, who see it as an act of needless gatekeeping. The experts do not claim to fully understand the proof yet, as it is too lengthy and complicated for human minds to immediately grasp.
